XCOM 2 is the supreme turn-based tactical role-playing game, and deservedly so. It is graphically perfect, story-rich, full of entertaining, believable characters, and is emotionally captivating. It is also one of the hardest games I’ve played. The developer, Firaxis, excelled at creating the ultimate challenge but made some inexplicable decisions that detract from the game and turn enjoyment into frustration, even for experienced game players. Despite this, it is possible to win the game. I have included some hints below:
Play as a ‘Rookie’ first time through – you will fail at the ‘Veteran’ level
Do not lose soldiers – extra skills and health are gained with promotions that come from killing multiple aliens over several missions. Your soldiers must survive
Improve weapons before armour – a dead alien can’t do any damage
Manage resources carefully – in the early stages, you need to do everything at once but have limited resources. Choose carefully
Choose Engineers over Scientists – Engineers are essential to progress, whereas scientific research goes faster than you can cope with 
Build a Workshop in a central location to get four Staffing Gremlins (net +2 engineers)
Build a ‘Guerrilla Tactics School’ as soon as possible - increase the number of soldiers in your squad from four to five, and eventually six
Reduce recovery time with an ‘Advanced Warfare Centre’ when you can
Rangers are winners – Rangers do twice as much damage as everyone but Sharpshooters. You need multiple experienced Rangers
Focus Specialist soldiers on healing – a properly equipped Specialist is needed on every mission; the higher the rank, the better
Use Psionic soldiers – build a Psi Lab when you can, as Psi operatives have uniquely powerful capabilities
Place Sharpshooters on elevated ground to get an accuracy boost
Mechanical fighters are optional – Sparks are strong but vulnerable, fun but unnecessary. Grenadiers with armour shredding are more versatile
A grapple is surprisingly useful, especially for Rangers, to increase their range
Mindshields are essential for every soldier, especially in the early stages
Hold off weapon modifications – more powerful weapons become available later, and enhancements cannot be swapped over
Break new ground with the first squad member – breaking new ground when no soldier has any moves left is a total disaster
Deal with a group of enemies before moving forward and encountering another group
Save at every mission start – if things go badly, you need to replay the mission. Autosaves get overwritten
Save regularly – the randomness of accuracy, critical hits and dodging can be partially overcome by trying a risky manoeuvre, and if it fails, reloading the game and doing something different
Don’t let the Avatar Project red dots fill completely, as this ends the game
Good luck, and try not to stress out.

So this game is quite an interesting one. I played and attempted it several times since I own and love X-Com Enemy Within. It bested me each time and left me in quite a seething rage at points. I decided to give it another go with the War of The Chosen expansion coming and I have to say that this game did finally win me over. This game can be brutally hard to you. It really expects you to take your time and think about your moves for the first half of the game. You get a little more leeway once you get to the second half and you have some vetern soldiers and their abilities. Let me address the most controversial topic first, the mission timers. 

       Coming from EW I hated them and it felt like they were everywhere. Having finally beaten the game I can say that it's roughly 50% of the missions are timed and I really came to enjoy them. They change up the primary tactic of move, overwatch and they make sense thematically.  I only lost one mission with them and that was my fault of not planning properly. There are mods on the workshop that alter them but I think you should give them a go as the developers intended first. They create a great sense of tension and you really have to evaluate your moves each turn. I love optimizing stuff and this really became great fun once I got the hang of them. Just expect to lose a few times while you learn how those missions play out.

       For those of you new to the Xcom series just know that these games run a reverse difficulty curve, they are hard in the beginning and get easier as the game progresses. Most the difficulty also comes from not knowing really where to begin. The game does not do a great job of making things clear to you. I did have to watch some videos and do some reading to really get a good grasp of the game. Also it doesn't make it clear what negative effects come from not attempting missions. I got a mission for a supply raid which I didn't attempt and the aliens ended up recapturing that territory. I didn't expect that and it wasn't communicated to me that that would be the result. The game likes to omit other valuable tacital data as well so I highly recommend the following mods:

Stop Wasting My Time
Show Health Values
Patrol When Revealed
Perfect Information
Gotcha

They save time in game but reducing certain animations and they really help you make informed moves each turn. I feel like Gotcha is a must have and something the developers should've included in the game to begin with. I'd also recommend some the communties mod map packs so you avoid getting 'familiar' maps. I also personally like It's Just A Scratch just because I think armor should actually protect you not just increase your health.

          This game ran smooth as butter the entire time with a couple of exceptions. When I destroyed lots of objects all at once and a couple times in the final mission. Otherwise I got a steady 60 fps and load times were between 5-30 seconds. It does have some minor bugs. The most frequent one I would get is where I would click on an ability and the character would instantly do it. Very annoying when I needed my last grenade for something useful. Also sometimes the character models can get inside of each other. Visually jarring but the game still treats them as being on seperate squares so not game breaking.

          Would I recommend you buy it? Absolutely, so long as you are ok losing a few times to learn the game. It's a fantastic strategy game and one of my personal favorites. What really got me with this game was how truly fair it actually did seem. Even in the face of overwhelming odds, smart tactical play saved me many times and it felt very rewarding. Honestly this game reminds me of dark souls a lot. It isn't just about the stats of your in game characters, it's about the knowledge you gain as well. I hope to see you out there Commander.

XCOM 2 is a turn-based strategy game with emphasis on tactical combat. It represents the eighth entry in the XCOM game series, and has been developed by the company Firaxis Games and published by the company 2K.

[i] Pro & contra: [/i]

++ Campaign playthrough is engaging and provides diversified side quests, with different mission goals and winning conditions. Excellent soundtrack keeps up the mood. Detail put into level design and environmental effects is impressive. Offers very high replayability.

++ The game encourages to recruit and build a highly specialised army, and the mechanics put in place for doing so are sophisticated. Base building and economics add another layer of challenge to the game. 

+ The narrative is well-delivered, with an even pace and solid character development. The player is likely to develop emotional attachment to some of the soldiers, increasing the immersion into the game. 

o Steep learning curve may deter casual gamers. In comparison with its predecessor the general level of difficulty is higher. For masochistic hardcore gamers the legendary ‘ironman’ mode is available.

o Missions are rng-based (random number generator), which could result in a lot of timed missions or almost no timed missions. [Thanks to Athena for mentioning this point.]

- Quite a few bugs and glitches, ranging from minor clipping issues to opponents shooting through obstacles. [Thanks to Volvox Globator for highlighting these points.]

- Occasional in-game slowdowns during certain events, e.g. pause between rounds, or calculation of burning effects. No optimization for 4K resolution causing irregular fps drops.

[i] Summary: [/i]

XCOM 2 offers a superb strategy experience, which manages to improve the original XCOM formula on every level.

[i] Achievements: [/i]

The game changes a lot with the difficulty you choose at the start of the campaign, your choice to enable or disable ironman-mode and the mods you installed.

So I write three shorties to rate the game properly. 

1. Game difficulty Recruit or Veteran
Only choose Recruit if you never played X-Com before and Veteran if you never played Wotc/Xcom 2 before. This difficulties are very easy and not challenging for players who understood the basic mechanics of the game already.

2. Commander
Choose this difficulty after you finished one Veteran-run. If you enable ironman-mode, this is exactly the gamestyle I recommend to play: It is challenging but fair. Unfair situations are a rare sight, so mostly only the player mistakes set the path for his downfall. You will fail a few times, but if you build up a deeper understanding of the game mechanics, you will succeed in the end. And it feels really good. 

3. Legendary
This difficulty seems to be broken for me. Sometimes you made no mistake in the whole mission and still got team wiped. And Xcom 2 have still some bugs. These bugs are no big deal on the first three difficulties. But on Legendary difficulty, which is already designed to be unfair sometimes, every bug is a game changer.

A list of the most annoying bugs:
a) Line of sight bug - Aliens can sometimes see throw walls and discover your concealed units.

b) Enemy occupies your rescue area with reaction fire or just a marker:
Normally if an enemy ENTERS your rescue area on a rescue mission, this area should be moved to another location. If an enemy with the marker ability marks one of your soldiers and you enter with this marked unit the rescue area, it also moves. Even if you enter the rescue area with a soldier who got shoot under reaction fire, the area moves.

c) Ice grenade:
If you use the ice grenade on an enemy, it is frozen for a few turns. If you somehow must use your ice grenade on an ally which is mind controlled, this ally is frozen forever.

-----------------------
I recommend the game on Commander/Ironman - this is a perfect experience. Only the very late game is easy because in the very end you should be overpowered.

Listen, there are three ways to play this game. Way #1 is to actually behave like a commander of a nearly-defunct resistance force, carefully scrutinizing the strengths and weaknesses of your enemies and creating units whose gear and abilities make them highly specialized for combating specific types of enemy, and thus giving your organization a chance at survival and victory Way #2 is to go full American military on it and get as many soldiers, guns, and gear as possible and brute force the aliens into submission, giving your soldiers the abilities and skills that make them as heavy damage dealing as possible.

Then there's way #3, the way I play, in which you're a blend of middle manager and dad. Every class of soldier can get subdivided into two general roles, denoted by colour-coded armor—and no, those roles don't always align with the dichotomy of the ability paths—which you begin associating with the soldiers, especially if you save their appearances for later games. When your soldiers are high enough rank to get nicknames, you give them a nickname based on what they do in their next mission, thereby giving them an identity and personality in your head beyond just their code. You start making headcanons of which soldiers get along with which others, why they got involved in this sort of thing, and so on. Eventually, you start cheering for them, berating them when they screw up, and being actively impressed when they pull off risky maneuvers. In short: you invest emotionally in your soldiers, and play the game in such a way to bring out their perceived talents. And boy howdy are you happy when you start a new game and a familiar face appears in the recruitment window.

Could I tell you about gameplay? Story? Okay. So i played the crap out of this game. As you can see at my play hours.
I understood and learned a bunch of things about it, so let's get started:

The game takes place 20 years after the Defeat of XCOM in the original game, going from a timeline where they lost their base at the hands on the alien Invasion. From there, they now work at a salvaged Alien Ship, from the looks of it seems to be one of the Heavy class ship of old. Earth is now subjugated and you are the leader of the resistance forces who fight against their rule. You, the Commander, must fight back against a new and sinister enemy know as ADVENT, an governemnt organization created by the Coalition between humans and the Alien Elders, while trying to stop a secret project that could be the end of mankind.

GAMEPLAY ASPECTS and thoughts on it:

> The RNG and POSITIONING
-Tactical based gameplay similar to the original game, but improved. More organized than the previous titles.
It requires not only strategic thinking to turn odds to your favor, but also a little bit of luck in a RNG dice roll. That said, the RNG is heavily influenced by how you are positioned and protected. 
You will not hit every shot, and the aliens can hit you with some lucky shots, however both of you are governed by the same rules, with the veteran difficulty balancing the tip towards your favor with "Miss Streaks" and "Aim Assists" for your soldiers. At higher difficulties, those differences cease, you and the aliens obey the same odds.
A bad positioning effectively means your defeat, and a strong positioning can lead you to victory. Keep that in mind while playing and you will find yourself depending less on luck and more in how you place your troops. (It may happen the hilarious 95% chance miss, it's not frequent and quite rare, unless the game really decided to hate you all of a sudden).

> SKILLS and ABILITIES
-Abilities are important, as they can bless you with guaranteed hits you will definetly need in some situations. It can turn the tide of battles very quickly to your favor. That said, the enemy can do the very same things with their abilities should the circunstances present themselves. Two units close to each may result in a grenade flying towards you. Or one of the powerful abilities the aliens have may be used against you.
With that in mind you will understand that some aliens must be taken out first, or that will result in one of your troopers being dragged across the map or half of your squad poisoned.
Different Aliens mean different aproach and different strategies, learn your enemy in order to defeat them.

> CLASSES and PROGRESS
- There are effectively 4 default classes for your troops with 1 special class divided in two ability trees that give them different roles in combat, the abilities can be mixed, so you are not stuck with just one role or the other, and given the proper infrastructure, you can retrain them (although you cannot change their class)

- The Aliens do have different types of enemies with different abilities, however their upgrades are based around the progression know as "force level" and "Dark Events". 
-> The force level effectively defines the type of alien you will face, as well as the upgrades towards aliens you already encounter. A common trooper will become and Advanced trooper as the time moves forward, and later in the game you will be facing Elite level troopers and more powerful Aliens.
-> Dark Events are strategic elements that rule over your campaign, they can last 1 to 2 months depending on the Event, or add points to their secret project. They can range from adding poison coated ammo to your enemies, or sent a UFO to hunt your SHIP.

>RESEARCH:
The research element is straight to the point, have a material, research it. Have a corpse, autopsy it. Have a thing, do this thing. You can improve your research time with more scientists.

>ENGINEERING:
Also straight to the point. You research a thing, you acquired a blueprint on that thing, you build that thing.
With the exception on the proving grounds, where takes time to construct an armor or make said blueprint. Experimental item blueprints give you a random item that can make a hell of a difference in your performance. Or building an more advanced armor that is not the default medium choice.

-TIP-
Research and Engineering can save you if you had your star squad wiped by a couple of bad decisions, however, losing missions over and over may result in campaign victory for the aliens, and you falling behind in force level category, where there's simply no way for you to face them anymore without you effectively turning a simple encounter into an epic struggle between untrained troops and powerful alien overlords. 
Which most of the time will result in Death if you are not of the most experienced XCOM player.

That said, these elements make an realistic representation in technology gap, if you don't keep up with your enemy, you will get steam rolled across the battlefield. It also means that if you manage to get the Early advantage in boosting your crew Engineers and Scientist staff, you will effectively do the same thing to them, although it all comes down in how you manage your squad into battle. Once you get the hang of it, you will rarely lose a mission, maybe a soldier or two.

>STORYLINE MISSIONS and OBJECTIVES:
- There are a couple of missions that represent the Storyline progression, which are required to complete in order to reach the end and win the game. Some have the term of "catasthropical failure", which results in instant victory for the aliens should you lose it. Missions with that term allow you to restart it and try again, or restart the game with a new campaign. One of the two.

--------- In regards to DLC -----------

Alien Hunters:
- This DLC adds four new powerful itens and three new powerful aliens for you to face along your campaign. With a story element should you decide to have the complete.
-> Having the story mode selected you will have a mission that starts the scenario, the enemies will not appear until you decide to.
-> Not having the story mode selected results in the enemies appearing normaly in the campaign and the weapons appearing in the engineering section for you to build them.

Shen's last gift:
- This DLC adds a MEC to your squad. An early game useless unit but a late game monster with the technological improvements. Like the Alien Hunters, it does have an story element that allows you to start the DLC. If not selected, you will be able to build it as soon as you get the Proving grounds.

Anarchy's Children:
- A cosmetic DLC, it adds anarchy themed cosmetics to the game for you soldiers customization. The flavour is not for everyone and honestly, you can find better mods for your cosmetics. Although it has a cool piece here and there, it doesn't justify a DLC.

Resistance warrior pack:
- Another cosmetic DLC, that in it's size, doesn't justify a DLC. And for some reason is not included in the reinforcement pack.

------- Personal suggestion for developers --------

If you are planning on making a DLC for the game, i would suggest one where we could play as the Aliens in their Storyline, it seems that it has a room for expansion and will allow for a different perspective. It would introduce an different aspect to the game since the we would be playing on the Aliens Side. and will allow for some player to have a choice to subjugate humanity, or not, depending what the aliens are really thinking.
It seems like a silly suggestion but it has room for potential if done correctly.

------- Overall ---------

It's a game that is supposed to be Brutal and unforgiving on combat side, any early mistake can lead to a defeat. It does get easier over time as you progress, but even so, it's not for casual or newbies that can't learn from their mistakes. Although Veterans can have a very casual experience.
Overall.
8 / 10 for Gameplay. 7 / 10 for Strategy. 4 / 10 for DLC. 7 / 10 for Story.

     To summarize, if you are not an expert at Xcom, then set it on rookie and possibly ironman for a fun game for people who enjoy strategy games and even consider themselves good at them.  Anything above rookie will not only kick your butt, but do so in a way that will make you hate the game.  This is not dark souls where dying does not detract from the experience. This game can make you very angry and stressed out. So do not be discouraged by the label of "rookie," even it can leave you with your entire squad wiped if you are not very careful.

The reason I say this is that there are many enemies that if you have not experienced, will destroy you in seemingly unfair ways.  If I had been bound and killed by a Viper on rookie ironman without knowing about them, I may have been very upset. However, I still lost my first Reaper unit to a Viper on my second rookie ironman playthrough with War of the Chosen, and continued to have fun and beat that playthrough.  The save-enabled playthrough simply let me learn to use tactics like attacking the Vipers before they can bind you, which I could then use on ironman without being confused as to how to handle them.

**To enable IRONMAN, you must disable the tuturial (at least in War of the Chosen).  This may be detrimental to new players, so you may want to play the tuturial level then restart the game if you are determined to try ironman right away.

This is a bit of a mixed review.  I'll be concise and explain the pros and cons:

Pros-
-  Really solid combat that improves greatly on XCOM 1/Enemy Unknown.

-  Good character customization which makes you invest a little in them instead of units just being placeholders.

-  Good variety of missions.  WotC expansion adds a great deal more.

-  WotC introduces a slew of voiceovers from Star Trek TNG alumni, which I love.

-  RNG missions keep the game fresh for a long time.

-  Workshop support really lets you reinvent entire portions of the game to make it more fun.  Everything from balance adjustments to new weapons models and sounds, character appearance changes, and even enemy unit changes is a welcome sight.

Cons-
-  2K launcher, which replaced the original some time ago, is a buggy mess.  As of this writing, I can't load the game at all, much less with mods.  The same launcher works for Civ VI just fine, so apparently just XCOM 2 is busted.

-  Horrible performance, even on a good rig.  This might be more of a HDD versus SSD issue, as I don't have SSD space to use and must rely on old mechanical drives instead, but XCOM 2 is lucky to keep 30-50 FPS on 1440/ultra on a 3080 GPU.  The GPU and CPU aren't even remotely taxed, so the issue must be crap programming or a non-SSD storage.  The latter would be absolute nonsense given that SSDs weren't commonplace when the game launched and larger ones used for gaming storage are still moderately pricey.  The sad truth is that an excess of mods makes this FPS stutter even worse, so be warned.

-  I've beaten the base game and expansion on vanilla before and recommend one solid pure playthrough, but ultimately every single replay for me involves modding the game to get more enjoyment out of diversified character appearance, weapon appearance, missions, and even enemy model replacements.  Given that the 2K launcher is busted, and the workaround involves not using mods at all, this selling point is a stopping point.  Currently I'm stuck at the end of a Legend difficulty playthrough because my cosmetic mods are enabled and the launcher won't launch period, much less enable my mods for continuity.

-  Being entirely fair here, a lot of the challenge comes from the enemy units just blatantly unfair in terms of their numbers, free movement and overwatch upon discovery, and things like timed missions and the greater time on the Avatar project (which forces you to rush the endgame hard).  This scales heavily with higher difficulty, to the point where I question the game logic entirely when six out of ten  shots against a target with 63-65% accuracy fail in a row.  That's not an exaggeration and no, I didn't buy a lotto ticket that day but I perhaps should have done so.

tl;dr I still love this game and I recommend it, but I advise newer players be aware of the faults it has and be prepared for the occasional frustration when something breaks because of bugs, a mod conflict, or 2k's crap launcher rendering it temporarily unplayable.

Xcom 2 is like playing a chess with a really great looking gameboard and chess pieces. Game is slow-paced and you are supposed to lose sometimes. If you are looking for fast action and immediately results this is not the game for you.

Core gameplay is solid gold. You can have up to 6 soldiers under your command per mission. Missions have different kind of goals and some require to be completed within 8 - 12 turns. Something like 3/5 missions have a turn timer but I didn't find it problematic as I nearly always had 2-3 turn "spare time" when I completed the mission goal. When people start dying it is often your own fault. There are total of 6 soldier classes, all with unique abilities and skills. Classes feels different with many combinations available how to assemble your squad. If you have played Xcom:EU you learn the new game mechanics within first few hours. All the enemies are new or atleast altered so you don't feel like playing Xcom: EU with a new plot.

Story is interesting and revealed by tiny pieces after completing missions and specific researches. There is a nice pacing with cutscenes and reading when moving forward the main plot. There ain't that many character in the game but they are all well written, besides that annoying little Shen.

In campaign map you make the big decisions: what recourses to get, what region to help, which missions to accept, where to build facilities, how to utilize your staff... You can't get everything, you usually choose what you need most at the time. Making these decions is the most rewarding part of the game. 

Xcom 2 is still plagued by performance and optimize issues even the game was launched more than
half year ago. Animations lags sometimes even with no action on the screen and they lag like hell when there are multiple fire/acid burning animations going on. Loading a mission can take up to a minute to load and returning to base takes the same. Pretty often there are 10 to 20 seconds "pauses" during alien turns when the game clearly think what it should do. It is also a pain to board the skyranger as in some missions you have to invidially move all units to extraction area and watch the painfully slow animation about your soldiers getting aboard. Sure this is a minor thing as almost every con in this game but when there are too many of these  annoying little things they really begin to affect your game experience. When game is turn-based = pretty slow going  you really don't like any additional issues to slow the game down.

There is also one extremely frustrating bug that I have to mention here. Sometimes your soldiers and aliens can shoot through floors/roof when there is accessible multiple-floor building in the map. This line of sight bug has been in Xcom 2 since launch. Some people even argue that it is a feature because "aliens have supernatural powers and roof has holes for you to shoot through". No this is not the case, building can be in perfect condition and no one is outside the building to give you vision on enemies but magically you see them loud and clear.

Overall game experience was not as satisfying as Xcom: EU was, still I strongly recomend to try this if you liked the predecessor. It took 30 hours to beat the game on veteran diffulty and game was enternaining right to the end. There are amazing variety of mods available so you can tweak the game to suit better your playstyle/taste. Played with no mods, Anarchy's child and Shen's last gift DLCs enabled and Alien hunter DLC disabled as I had read some horrible feedback about the second DLC.

[u] Summary: [/u]
The game that has everything going for it as a sequel to one of the best reborn franchises of the last 5 years.....with one huge exception. The tactical combat from the original returns with some additional units and mechanics that takes it to the next level. The small changes like additional focus on timed missions helped the game in the big picture a lot, and the improved balance/skill trees made every class a great boon in the right situation. The simulation portion of the game may have been streamlined....but it was for the better in my opinion, as it makes an impact on your combat performance directly. The visuals for the most part are nice, although it will take you out the experience as well with some bad glitches. The story makes a bit more sense this time around and while its filled with scifi tropes, it does the job. This would be a shoe-in purchase if the performance issues, load times, and glitches are taken care of, because they REALLY create a major problem in the end, as I would have stopped playing if I wasn't formal reviewing the game. If you've got a backlog: play through it first, and wait for some of the issues to be fixed. 

[b] Review Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dsQH16fF9Dc [/b]

[u] Lists: [/u]
[b]Positives:[/b]
[list]
[*] The well known combat is still as good as ever, with incremental improvements. Difficult but smartly put together.
[*] Class balance seems to be there a bit more this time around..Psy operatives were useful and still strong, but a great grenadier or ranger could give them a run for their money.
[*] Simulation elements wisely refined, and seemed to make the difference in the battle in the long run.
[*] Like the addition of more timed missions: it forces  less conservative play, and put your units more in danger, but not to the point where it was unwinnable.  
[*] Great character customization added that makes the sting of losing a soldier that much harder, when you've put the effort in crafting them from the bottom up. Your soldiers also can have a nice in-game personality that actually shows up in the lines. 
[*] Great move on Firaxis part to put in mod support on day one. I expect a lot to be done, as there's a lot of potential in the various weapons/units/etc. 
[*] The secondary equipment makes a huge difference this time around, and there was actually huge reasons to take it along as opposed to another med pack. 
[*] Improved visuals, in particular with character designs. Like the simple yet effective designs of the Viper and the Gatekeeper.
[*] For those who really want it, Firaxis put several autosaves in there at the start of a mission and last turn. If you're a cheater. Cause it's cheating. 

[/list]

[b]Negatives:[/b]
[list]
[*] Hate, hate the new graze system. It adds an element to combat that you don't know what it directly does in terms of percent probability for it to happen, and is generally an unknown factor. It's the one thing you don't know, and it will REALLY get on your nerves.
[*] Panic system seems to mean less then before.
[*] Held together by glue and string, it seems. The game can run great at times, but when something goes wrong, bad things happen to not only the performance, but the in game mechanics get messed with as well. It's unstable. 
[*] The loading times. My god the loading times. At one point, it took 3 minutes,  27 seconds to load into the next portion of the game. Unoptimized, the game is not. 
[*] Glitch Fest 2000. Hits a wide spectrum of issues, from graphical, to camera, to in-game affecting. Takes you right of the experience. It's funny at times....but really annoying at others. Especially when the camera decides to show you a wall because it can't figure out jack shit.

In my opinion, XCOM2 is a masterpiece in the turn-based strategy genre. The game revolves around the classic battle against malevolent, invasive aliens. The primary focus is on creating, upgrading, and equipping a squad of fighters for combat missions while prioritizing the construction and expansion of rooms within the "Avenger," an alien ship that serves as your base of operations. The missions, typical of turn-based games, require intelligent positioning and the effective use of each squad member's abilities.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is not particularly deep and is kept relatively short, though it does follow a coherent thread. Depending on your taste, this might seem a bit lacking, but for me, it worked well as it left more room for the action. The narrative is partially woven into the missions, which adds a nice touch to the overall experience.

[h1]Combat[/h1]
The battles are always fair and gain additional dynamism through random placements. While specific tactics generally prove effective, there are moments that demand creative solutions, which is a clear plus in my book. The difficulty level is highly customizable, and for those seeking a real challenge (like myself), the Ironman mode offers an intense and rewarding experience.

[h1]Progression[/h1]
The progression system is extremely motivating, as you earn new equipment and upgrade your squad. There isn't a vast amount of gear, which some might see as a downside, but it was fine for me. The sense of growth and improvement keeps you engaged, although the limited variety of equipment might be a minor drawback for some players.

[h1]Atmosphere and Design[/h1]
Both the design of the units and the environments are superbly executed. The atmosphere is incredibly well-crafted, immersing you deeply into the game and making each mission a thrilling experience. The detailed visuals, combined with the game's aesthetic, create a mood that keeps you engaged and excited to dive back into the action.

[h1]Gameplay and Technical Performance[/h1]
The gameplay, stability, and controls are excellent, with almost no bugs to speak of. The core mechanics are solid, and the overall experience is smooth and enjoyable, which is a testament to the game's polish.

[h1]Replay Value[/h1]
The replay value is average; while there is some potential for replaying, it can feel exhausted after a certain point—especially if you compare it to games like Civilization. However, the game offers enough content to keep you entertained for a good amount of time before this happens.

[h1]Classes and Character Bonding[/h1]
The class selection in the base game is somewhat limited, but it improves significantly with the addition of the "War of the Chosen" expansion. Personally, I found the bond with my characters to be very strong, although this can vary from player to player. I also enjoyed the customization options (cosmetics), which added an extra layer of fun.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Overall, I would rate XCOM2 a solid [b]4.5 / 5[/b]. With the "War of the Chosen" expansion, it truly becomes a masterpiece, offering an even richer and more satisfying experience [b]5 / 5[/b].

XCOM 2 is essentially XCOM 1 with everything dialed up a notch. The short of it is that if you liked and played XCOM 1 for any significant amount of time then you are almost guaranteed to enjoy XCOM 2.

[h1]Great new additions or significant improvements:[/h1]

[b][u]RNG:[/u][/b] The huge role random chance played in the core mechanics of XCOM 1 was something that really bothered me and many other players. Thankfully, in this iteration, there are so many more ways of dealing guaranteeing damage that it is relatively simple to mitigate RNG almost completely with the appropriate style of play. A few things allow this: first off more abilities that are guaranteed to deal damage including combat protocol on the specialist and weapon upgrades that deal dmg on missed shots, cover is more destructible this time around which allows you to easily expose enemies for reliable shots and most importantly the way the game works now allows and even encourages aggressive flanking. It is not uncommon to get 90-100% shot success on most missions mid way through the campaign now as a result.

[b][u]Aggression and overwatch spam:[/u][/b] Due to the way the maps were configured and the constant threat of activating additional groups of enemies, a very defense oriented and overwatch centered tactical play style was considered optimal in XCOM 1. This is entirely not the case in XCOM 2. The way the maps are setup now, it feels like you have much more room to maneuver around the map without fatally exposing your squad. With the concealment mechanic which lets you sneak up on the aliens and with the presence of turn limits on many more missions this time around, the game actually encourages an aggressive playstyle where you take out enemy groups with 1-2 turns of activating them through aggressive flanking and, as is my preference, heavy use of explosives. Another important aspect of this is that using explosives no longer equates to losing the loot you desperately need to fund your operations. It’s a little bit more complicated than that but generally speaking you don’t have to stress so much about not blowing up the aliens this time around.

[b][u]Additional customization options:[/u][/b] I really wasn’t into tweaking the appearance of my soldiers in XCOM 1 that much but with the mind blowing amount of customization options available now, I’m really getting attached to some of my soldiers that I’ve decked out to look badass. The character pool system which lets saved soldiers randomly appear in your campaign as recruits or VIPs or scientists and engineers is also quite brilliant and unexpected allowing for favorite soldiers to effortlessly reappear in a new campaign. With the out of the box support for mods through steam workshop, the already staggering number of options will only grow.

[h1]Things which are problematic:[/h1]

[b][u]Unresponsiveness:[/u][/b] I had this complaint with XCOM 1 as well. What I’m talking about is how the game loves to take control away from you in the middle of the action, locking the camera and disabling input while it makes you stare at a “new” enemy that you’ve already seen before accompanied by Central or the Doctor essentially telling you what you most likely already know. There is seemingly more of that this time around and some abilities, in particular gremlin abilities on the specialist have unnecessarily long animations for you to endure. Some of this also applies to the UI in the macro game (the avenger and geoscape). Transferring from the geoscape to the armory menu for instance, take entirely too long and clicking while the animation is in progress may end up sending you to another menu accidentally which only serves to frustrate the matter more.

[b][u]UI streamlining:[/u][/b] In the course of trying to make the UI less dense, a lot of useful information has been buried further down in menus. This leads to a lot of unnecessary clicking to find important bits of information and makes comparing some stats across soldiers unjustifiably painful. The biggest culprit of course, is not being able to see vital soldier stats side by side across soldiers, including their hp and what upgrades they have installed on themselves and their gear. There are several other places where the streamlined approach makes information difficult to discern or understand due to ambiguity, but all this one can get used to eventually, even though some frustration will be encountered along the way. I suspect this is once again a symptom of PC games being constrained by a UI designed for a controller. It’s not a major gripe, but it is something which should have been improved in this iteration and not the other way around as it stands now.

THE BAD:
- The beginning of the game, with all the DLC included, has an overwhelming amount of stuff going on.
- There was a point in the game where I started falling behind the aliens in terms of advancement, and I either would have had to restart (wasting 20 hours of play time) or save scum. I chose save scumming, but it did break immersion somewhat.
- The great graphics are marred by clipping issues. E.g. I've a seen soldier shoot their friend through the head to hit an alien on the other side (without injuring their friend), a soldier walk off a cliff to take a shot (floating in mid-air) and then return, and soldiers routinely move their guns through obstacles and fire bullets through impossible obstacles like concrete or the lengths of cars.
